title: The internet runs on cats: what the research says
description: Cats are the internet's unofficial mascot, and the programmer with a cat on the desk is a stereotype. But do tech people really prefer cats? Along the way you'll meet the neural network that learned "cat" without anyone telling it what a cat was, a survey of nearly 7,000 people about why they watch cat videos, an Ig Nobel prize for asking whether cats are liquid, and software that locks your keyboard when a cat walks on it. Each Question sorts the fun claim from what the evidence supports.
author: Quizbun

questions.title: Is there solid evidence that people in IT like cats more than other people do?

options.text: No. The largest developer survey we found leaned toward dogs, and it had no non-developers to compare with
Yes. Stack Overflow's developer survey shows it every year
Yes. A 2014 personality study of programmers proved it
No. Studies show IT people are allergic to cats more often

questions.explanation:
Stack Overflow asked "Dogs or cats?" in its 2016 Developer Survey. Of the 45,239 respondents who answered, 48.9% picked dogs, 34.8% cats and 16.4% something else. Germany went the other way, with cats ahead of dogs.

Even so, that survey can't answer this Question. "More than other people" needs a comparison, and nobody outside software answered the same survey. A dog-leaning result among developers fits with developers liking cats *more* than the general public, *less*, or the same. We didn't find any large study that compares pet preference across jobs. That doesn't prove no such study exists, so read the stereotype as unproven rather than disproved.

As far as we can tell, it's a cultural joke with no evidence behind it.
questions.references: [Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2016: overview](https://survey.stackoverflow.co/2016/), [Stack Overflow 2016 raw results (CSV, column `dogs_vs_cats`)](https://github.com/StackExchange/Survey/tree/main/packages/archive/2016)

images.alt: Bar chart of the 2016 Stack Overflow survey question "Dogs or cats?". All 45,239 respondents: dogs 48.9%, cats 34.8%, other 16.4%. Germany, 3,154 respondents: dogs 38.4%, cats 44.5%, other 17.0%. A note says only developers answered, so the chart cannot compare developers with anyone else.
images.caption: Percentages computed from Stack Overflow's published 2016 raw data, counting only people who answered the question. Chart drawn for this Quiz.

questions.title: What kind of study could show whether IT workers like cats more than other people do?

options.text: A representative survey of many occupations that asks everyone the same pet question, then compares IT workers with the rest
A poll on a programming forum asking members whether they like cats
Counting cat photos in developers' social media posts
Interviewing a dozen well-known programmers about their pets

questions.explanation:
The claim compares two groups, so the study needs both groups, measured the same way.

- **A comparison group.** A forum poll only reaches programmers. Even a perfect result tells you what programmers like, not whether they like it *more*.
- **Representative sampling.** People decide for themselves whether to answer a forum poll or post cat photos, and cat lovers are more likely to do both. That inflates the result.
- **The same measure for everyone.** Counting photos measures posting habits. Cats may just be easier than dogs to photograph at a desk.

Interviewing famous programmers gives you a handful of memorable cases, which is how stereotypes form in the first place. Only the first design gets you past anecdotes.

questions.title: A 2014 study reported that self-described "cat people" were more introverted than "dog people". Which of these limit what it can tell us about programmers?
questions.description: Psychologist Denise Guastello of Carroll University surveyed about 600 college students on their pet preference and personality.

options.text: The participants were college students, not workers in IT or any other field
Pet preference and personality were both self-reported on questionnaires
It found an association, which can't show whether cats make people introverted, introverts choose cats, or neither
About 600 people is too few for any statistical test to work
Introversion was measured with brain scans, which are known to be unreliable

questions.explanation:
The study asked students whether they saw themselves as dog lovers or cat lovers, then gave them personality questionnaires. Dog lovers scored as more energetic and outgoing. Cat lovers scored as more introverted, open-minded and sensitive.

Getting from there to "programmers like cats" takes two leaps the data doesn't support. First, students aren't programmers, and the study didn't ask about jobs. Second, even if programmers are more introverted on average, a link between introversion and cats among students doesn't automatically hold for a different group.

Six hundred people is plenty to detect a moderate difference between groups, so sample size isn't the issue. The issues are *who* took part and *what kind* of evidence it is: self-reported and correlational. Nobody scanned a brain or watched how anyone behaved.

So the evidence that cat people are more introverted comes down to one correlational survey of students.
questions.references: [Wikipedia: Cat people and dog people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cat_people_and_dog_people), [CBS News: "Dog people" and "cat people" have different personality traits (2014)](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/dog-people-and-cat-people-have-different-personality-traits-study-finds/), [Wikipedia: Correlation does not imply causation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Correlation_does_not_imply_causation)

questions.title: In 2012, a Google network learned to detect cats from YouTube stills. How many of its training images were labeled "cat"?

options.text: None
About 10,000
About half of them
All of them, because it was only shown cats

questions.explanation:
None at all. The training set was 10 million frames, one from each of 10 million YouTube videos, with no labels of any kind. This is called **unsupervised learning**.

The network was a sparse autoencoder. Its only job was to rebuild each input image after squeezing it through layers that could keep just a few features active at a time. To do that well on YouTube frames, it had to find patterns that show up often. Human faces are one, and cat faces turned out to be another. After training, the researchers searched the top layer for neurons that reacted to test images of cats, and one reacted strongly. Nobody told the network what a cat was. It picked up the concept from the data.

Labels came in only for a separate test: recognizing 22,000 ImageNet categories. There, the researchers used labeled examples to train a classifier on top of the features the network had learned.
questions.references: [Le et al. (2012): Building high-level features using large scale unsupervised learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/1112.6209), [Google blog: Using large-scale brain simulations for machine learning and A.I. (2012)](https://blog.google/technology/ai/using-large-scale-brain-simulations-for/), [Wikipedia: Autoencoder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autoencoder)

images.alt: Three boxes joined by arrows. First: 10 million frames, one per YouTube video, 200 by 200 pixels, no labels at all. Second: a 9-layer sparse autoencoder with about 1 billion connections, trained on 16,000 cores for 3 days. Third: one top-layer neuron fires strongly for cat faces, with others for human faces and bodies. A note says the training goal was to rebuild each input image from a compressed, sparse code.
images.caption: Figures from Le et al. (2012). Diagram drawn for this Quiz; the paper's own visualization of the cat neuron is linked in References rather than copied.

questions.title: What hardware did Google's 2012 cat-detecting network train on?

options.text: A cluster of 1,000 machines with 16,000 CPU cores, for three days
A single high-end gaming GPU, overnight
Sixteen machines with one GPU each, for a month
A laptop, because the network had only a few thousand connections

questions.explanation:
The model had about 1 billion connections and trained on 10 million images of 200 × 200 pixels. That was too big for one machine, so the team split the model across machines (model parallelism). They also ran many copies at once, each sending updates to shared parameter servers (asynchronous SGD). The whole job took 1,000 machines and 16,000 CPU cores for three days.

The GPU answers are tempting because GPUs run almost all deep learning today. In 2012 they were only starting to take over. That same year, AlexNet won the ImageNet competition on two GPUs, and that result did far more to change how people train networks.

The team went this big to answer the paper's main question: with a large enough model and dataset, can you learn high-level concepts from unlabeled data at all?

questions.title: The cat test set was about 35% cat faces and 65% other images. What accuracy, in percent, does a lazy classifier get by answering "not a cat" every time?
questions.description: The paper's face test had 13,026 positives among 37,000 images, and the cat test used the same ratio. Round to one decimal place.
questions.explanation:
Using the face test's counts, 23,974 negatives ÷ 37,000 images ≈ 0.648. Answering "not a cat" every time scores **64.8%** without looking at a single pixel. The paper lists exactly this as its "random guess" baseline.

Keep that number in mind when you hear about the famous cat neuron. Its best accuracy was **74.8%**, about 10 points above doing nothing and 7.6 points above the best simple linear filter (67.2%). The face neuron did better, at 81.7%, and a human-body neuron reached 76.7%.

For a network that had never seen a label, that was an impressive result in 2012. Still, a headline accuracy means little until you know what the do-nothing baseline scores. Whenever a test has unbalanced classes, check the baseline first.

The evidence that the network learned a cat concept is strong. As a detector, though, it was modest and far from reliable.
questions.references: [Le et al. (2012), Section 5 and Table 1](https://arxiv.org/abs/1112.6209), [Wikipedia: Accuracy paradox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accuracy_paradox)

images.alt: Bar chart on a 0 to 100 percent axis. Always answering "not a cat": 64.8%. Best simple linear filter: 67.2%. Best cat neuron: 74.8%. A dashed line at 64.8% marks accuracy that needs no learning.
images.caption: Numbers from Table 1 of Le et al. (2012). Chart drawn for this Quiz.

questions.title: Besides cat faces, which concepts did the 2012 paper report neurons responding to?

options.text: Human faces
Human bodies
Dogs
Written text

questions.explanation:
The paper is mostly about **faces**. It started by asking whether you could learn a face detector from unlabeled images, and its best face neuron scored 81.7%. The authors then checked whether other things common on YouTube had been learned too. They built two more test sets, found a **cat-face** neuron (74.8%) and a **human-body** neuron (76.7%), and stopped there.

The paper doesn't mention dogs or text because the authors never tested for them. That's different from finding that the network didn't learn them. A dog neuron may or may not have existed; nobody looked.

Cats made the headlines because they're funnier than faces. Before you retell a result, check what the research was mainly about.
questions.references: [Le et al. (2012), Sections 4 and 5](https://arxiv.org/abs/1112.6209), [NPR: A massive Google network learns to identify — cats (2012)](https://www.npr.org/2012/06/26/155792609/a-massive-google-network-learns-to-identify)

questions.title: In 2015, media researcher Jessica Myrick surveyed nearly 7,000 people about watching cat videos online. How did the survey reach them?

options.text: Mostly through social media, helped by the owner of Lil Bub, a celebrity internet cat
A random telephone sample of U.S. households
Students in an introductory psychology course
Volunteers randomly assigned to watch cat or dog videos in a lab

questions.explanation:
Lil Bub's owner, Mike Bridavsky, helped spread the survey on social media, and 6,795 people answered. That got a large sample quickly, but it's a sample of people who follow a famous cat online.

Keep that in mind for everything the survey found. A large sample shrinks random error, but it doesn't fix **selection bias**. Seven thousand cat fans can tell you a lot about cat fans and much less about everyone else. Only the lab option could test cause and effect. Random assignment is what separates "cat videos change mood" from "people in a certain mood look for cat videos", and this study didn't use it.

Myrick's study is a useful published survey. Just remember who answered it as you go through the next three Questions.
questions.references: [Myrick (2015), Computers in Human Behavior 52: Emotion regulation, procrastination, and watching cat videos online](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chb.2015.06.001), [ScienceDaily: Viewing cat videos boosts energy, positive emotions (2015)](https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2015/06/150616093357.htm), [Wikipedia: Selection bias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selection_bias)

questions.title: What did respondents in Myrick's survey report about how they felt after watching cat videos?

options.text: More energetic
More positive
Less anxious, annoyed and sad
Measurably more productive at work afterward
A lower heart rate

questions.explanation:
Respondents said they felt more energetic and more positive after watching cat videos than before. They also reported fewer negative emotions such as anxiety, annoyance and sadness.

Notice the word *reported*. These were answers to a one-time online survey. Nobody took anyone's pulse or measured their work output. The press release suggests the mood boost *may* help people take on hard tasks afterward, but that's a hypothesis the study didn't test.

Surveys like this are good for learning how people experience something and weak for learning what it does to them. Here, the evidence that cat videos lift mood is self-reported and comes from a self-selected group of cat fans.
questions.references: [ScienceDaily: Viewing cat videos boosts energy, positive emotions (2015)](https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2015/06/150616093357.htm), [Wikipedia: Self-report study](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-report_study)

questions.title: Many respondents watched cat videos at work or while studying. How did they describe the guilt of procrastinating?

options.text: They felt some guilt, but the enjoyment outweighed it
They felt no guilt at all
The guilt outweighed the enjoyment, so they felt worse overall
The survey didn't ask about guilt

questions.explanation:
The survey asked about guilt because the study was as much about procrastination and managing emotions as about cats. Respondents did feel guilty about watching when they should have been working or studying, but they said the fun outweighed the guilt.

Most of this viewing was passive. Only about a quarter of the cat videos people watched were ones they had searched for. They stumbled on the rest in feeds and on sites like Facebook, YouTube and BuzzFeed.

If you're reading this at work, you're in good company, according to people who were also reading about cats at work.
questions.references: [ScienceDaily: Viewing cat videos boosts energy, positive emotions (2015)](https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2015/06/150616093357.htm), [Wikipedia: Procrastination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Procrastination)

questions.title: According to Myrick's survey, who was more likely to watch cat videos?

options.text: People who own or have owned cats
People who scored higher on agreeableness
People who scored higher on shyness
People who work in IT

questions.explanation:
Current and past cat owners watched more, and so did respondents who scored higher on agreeableness and shyness. About 36% of respondents called themselves "cat people", and 60% said they liked both cats and dogs.

The IT option is the stereotype sneaking back in. The published summaries of the study say nothing about jobs, so the survey can neither support nor rule it out.

These are associations within an unusual sample. "Shy people watch more cat videos" is a fair summary of the data. "Cat videos attract shy people" and "cat videos make people shy" are cause-and-effect stories this design can't tell apart.
questions.references: [ScienceDaily: Viewing cat videos boosts energy, positive emotions (2015)](https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2015/06/150616093357.htm), [Wikipedia: Agreeableness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agreeableness)

questions.title: A physicist asked whether cats are liquids. What decides the answer?

options.text: How long you watch: over minutes a cat flows to fill its container, but in a snapshot it keeps its shape
The cat's body temperature
Whether the container is glass or ceramic
Nothing. The paper was a joke with no physics in it

questions.explanation:
Marc-Antoine Fardin studies rheology, the science of how materials flow and change shape. He started from a practical definition: a liquid changes its shape to fit its container. Plenty of photos online show cats doing exactly that in sinks, boxes and jars.

Whether something counts as a liquid depends on the **timescale**. Every material has a *relaxation time*, roughly how long it takes to adapt its shape. Divide that by how long you watch and you get the **Deborah number**, *De*. Below 1, the material flows while you watch, so it behaves like a liquid. Above 1, it keeps its shape, so it behaves like a solid. Glaciers flow over years. Silly Putty bounces when you throw it but slumps into a puddle over hours.

A cat that settles into a sink over a few minutes is a liquid on that timescale. The same cat in a 1/100 s photo is a solid.

Don't fall for the last Option. Fardin's paper, *On the rheology of cats* (Rheology Bulletin, 2014), is playful, but the rheology in it is real, and it won the **2017 Ig Nobel Prize in Physics**.

So are cats liquid? It depends on how long you watch, and that's the whole point.
questions.references: [Fardin in The Conversation: Answering the question that won me the Ig Nobel Prize: are cats liquid?](https://theconversation.com/answering-the-question-that-won-me-the-ig-nobel-prize-are-cats-liquid-86589), [Fardin (2014): On the rheology of cats, annotated at Fermat's Library](https://fermatslibrary.com/s/on-the-rheology-of-cats), [Wikipedia: Deborah number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deborah_number)

images.alt: A tabby-and-white cat asleep in a bathroom sink, curled so tightly that its body follows the round curve of the basin.
images.caption: Photo by Anagoria, [CC BY 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0/), via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:20190410_230530_Cat_Lissy_in_Bathroom_Sink_anagoria.jpg).

images.alt: A logarithmic scale of the Deborah number from 0.001 to 10,000, split at 1. Left of 1 is labeled "it flows (liquid)", right of 1 "it keeps its shape (solid)". A cat napping in a sink for an hour sits at about 0.017, on the liquid side. A cat in a 1/100 second photo sits at 6,000, on the solid side. A note says the example assumes a cat takes about 1 minute to settle into a container.
images.caption: De = relaxation time ÷ observation time. The one-minute relaxation time is an assumption for illustration. Diagram drawn for this Quiz.

questions.title: Suppose a kitten takes about 1 minute to settle into the shape of a box. If you watch it for 10 seconds, is it a liquid or a solid?
questions.description: Use De = relaxation time ÷ observation time, where De < 1 means it flows and De > 1 means it keeps its shape.

options.text: A solid: De = 60 ÷ 10 = 6, so it can't change shape in time
A liquid: De = 10 ÷ 60 ≈ 0.17, so it flows
A liquid, because kittens are softer than adult cats
Neither: De is exactly 1 for any living animal

questions.explanation:
Relaxation time goes on top: 60 s ÷ 10 s = **6**. That's greater than 1, so in a 10-second look the kitten doesn't have time to change shape. On that timescale, it's a solid.

The tempting wrong answer flips the fraction. Both numbers are in seconds, so the units won't catch the mistake. To remember the order, think of the extremes. A very long observation should push De toward zero and let everything flow, like mountains over geological time. That only works when observation time is on the bottom.

Watch the same kitten for an hour and De = 60 ÷ 3,600 ≈ 0.017, so it's a liquid. The kitten stayed the same; only your watching time changed.
questions.references: [Wikipedia: Deborah number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deborah_number), [Fardin in The Conversation: are cats liquid?](https://theconversation.com/answering-the-question-that-won-me-the-ig-nobel-prize-are-cats-liquid-86589)

images.alt: A black kitten lying in a shallow cardboard box on tissue paper, its body filling one end of the box.
images.caption: Photo by Catboy69, [CC0](https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/), via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cat_in_a_box_3.jpg).

questions.title: PawSense is software that notices when a cat walks across your keyboard. How does it tell a cat from a person?

options.text: It analyzes which keys are pressed together and the timing between presses
It watches through the webcam for fur
It detects body heat through the keys
It listens through the microphone for purring

questions.explanation:
PawSense works with the only data a keyboard gives it: which keys went down, in what combinations, and when. People press one key at a time, mostly in word-like bursts. A paw presses a clump of neighboring keys almost at once, with a rhythm no typist produces. Its maker says it usually spots a cat within one or two pawsteps.

Once it spots one, PawSense blocks the cat's input so the random keypresses never reach your programs. It also plays a sound that annoys cats, so they learn to stay off the keyboard even when nobody is around.

This is classification from behavior. PawSense needs no camera or special hardware, only patterns in ordinary input. Fraud detection and bot detection often work the same way, using typing rhythm and click timing.

images.alt: Two keyboards side by side. On the left, a person typing "cat" presses C, then A, then T, one key at a time and far apart; the timeline below shows three evenly spaced key-down events. On the right, a paw presses six neighboring keys, D, F, G, C, V and B, at almost the same moment; its timeline shows a tight burst of events.
images.caption: An illustration of the kind of signal PawSense reads, not its actual algorithm. Drawn for this Quiz.

questions.title: PawSense won the Ig Nobel Prize in Computer Science in 2000. What are the Ig Nobel Prizes for?

options.text: Achievements that first make people laugh, and then make them think
Mocking research that is useless or fraudulent
Research that failed peer review but deserved a second look
The funniest papers, as chosen by the Nobel Foundation

questions.explanation:
The Ig Nobels "honor achievements that first make people laugh, and then make them think". The *Annals of Improbable Research* has run them since 1991, and they have nothing to do with the Nobel Foundation.

Most winners are real, published work with an odd or funny angle. Chris Niswander won for PawSense in 2000, and Marc-Antoine Fardin's rheology of cats won the Physics prize in 2017. You laugh at the question, then start thinking once you see someone take it seriously: timescales in materials for Fardin, classification from input patterns for PawSense.

The mocking Option isn't entirely wrong. A few prizes have gone out ironically, as criticism. Those are exceptions, and neither cat prize is one of them.
questions.references: [Wikipedia: Ig Nobel Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ig_Nobel_Prize), [Wikipedia: List of Ig Nobel Prize winners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Ig_Nobel_Prize_winners)

questions.title: The Unix `cat` command isn't named after the animal. Type the word it's short for.
questions.explanation:
The manual page says so directly: `cat - concatenate files and print on the standard output`. *Concatenate* means to join things end to end, and that's the command's real job:

```bash
cat part1.txt part2.txt > whole.txt
```

Printing one file with `cat notes.txt` is just concatenation with a single file.

Because `cat` is so familiar, people often pipe it into commands that could read the file on their own, like `cat log.txt | grep error` instead of `grep error log.txt`. Unix folklore calls this a "useless use of cat". It does no harm in a terminal, though it does start an extra process.

Try it: open a terminal and run `man cat`.

questions.title: GitHub's mascot, the Octocat, began as stock clip art. What had its designer, Simon Oxley, called it?

options.text: Octopuss
Gitty
Kraken Kitty
Tentacat

questions.explanation:
Oxley drew a cat's head with octopus tentacles and sold it on iStock as **Octopuss**, from *octopus* plus *pussycat*. GitHub's founders found it while looking for an image for the site, negotiated exclusive rights with Oxley, and renamed it the Octocat.

It's a good reminder that stock images come with license terms. Putting clip art on a website and building a brand around it are different uses, and the second one took an agreement with the artist.

The Octocat also adds one more cat to the "programmers love cats" story. It makes the stereotype fun and easy to see, and as the earlier Questions showed, seeing something often doesn't make it proven.

questions.title: Which of these claims does the evidence in this Quiz support?

options.text: A neural network can learn to detect cat faces better than a do-nothing baseline without ever seeing a labeled cat
In Stack Overflow's 2016 survey, more responding developers picked dogs than cats
Whether a cat behaves as a liquid depends on how long you observe it
Developers like cats more than the general public does
Watching cat videos makes office workers more productive
Owning a cat makes people more introverted

questions.explanation:
Each supported claim rests on evidence that matches its wording.

- **Cat detector.** A published experiment with a held-out test set. The best cat neuron scored 74.8% against a 64.8% baseline, a modest but real gain.
- **Dogs versus cats.** Stack Overflow's own data, 48.9% to 34.8%. The claim stays inside what was measured: developers who answered one survey in 2016.
- **Liquid cats.** The Deborah number follows from the definitions. Watch long enough and the cat flows; watch briefly and it doesn't.

The unsupported claims overreach in familiar ways.

- **Developers versus the public.** This needs a comparison group, and no study we found has one.
- **Productivity.** Nobody measured it. Myrick's respondents *reported* a better mood, and they were cat fans reached through a celebrity cat's followers.
- **Cats cause introversion.** This turns a correlation among college students into cause and effect.

That's the habit this Quiz is trying to build: before you repeat a fun claim, ask what evidence it rests on and whether the claim stays within it.
questions.references: [Le et al. (2012)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1112.6209), [Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2016](https://survey.stackoverflow.co/2016/), [ScienceDaily: Myrick cat video study (2015)](https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2015/06/150616093357.htm), [Wikipedia: Deborah number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deborah_number)
